Scope
This document is the authoritative specification of the study’s scientific objectives, populations, definitions and statistical methods. ARCHITECTURE.md documents the implementation, AGENTS.md the working conventions, and GitHub Issues the open decisions and implementation status. Neither file supersedes this plan.
Reproduction rule. The rebuilt code reproduces the published numbers. Where the paper and the original code differ, the code that produced the published numbers is followed, and the difference is recorded on the website’s “Differences from the original code” page. Any change from what was published is a decision for the decider (AGENTS.md), made in a decision issue.

1. Objective
To evaluate whether a multispecialty educational intervention, delivered at a single transplant center in December 2020, was followed by greater acceptance of organs from deceased donors with HIV (D+) for candidates with HIV (R+) under the HOPE Act, and by a higher rate of transplantation among the center’s HOPE candidates.
Questions, as in the paper (Swaminathan et al. 2025):

Did the proportion of declined D+ offers declined for potentially HIV-related reasons fall after the intervention? (Primary offer-level measure.)
Did the share of offers provisionally accepted, and the share that became D+/R+ transplants at the center, change?
Among declined offers, how often was the donor’s organ transplanted elsewhere, before and after, overall and for potentially HIV-related declines?
Did the rate of transplants per patient-year on the waiting list change, for all transplants and for D+/R+ transplants?
How did candidates who were not transplanted, transplanted from D+ donors, and transplanted from D− donors compare, and how did the D+ and D− transplants compare?

No hypotheses were registered before the analysis. All questions are reported as in the paper; none is a confirmatory test.

2. Design
A single-center before-and-after comparison of a quality-improvement intervention: a pre-intervention period (March 2018 to November 2020) and a post-intervention period (December 2020 to April 2022), as stated in the paper. The intervention itself, and how its barriers were identified, are described in the paper and are not part of this analysis. The design cannot separate the intervention’s effect from national trends in the use of D+ organs over the same period; this is a limitation (section 11), not an estimand.

Two restricted values were removed from the code for patient privacy and are kept with the data (section 10): the intervention date, which is day 0 for both periods, and one record-level correction.
Linkage: offers are linked to candidates’ study IDs by candidate last name, as in the original code. An identifier would be better practice; names are used only inside the join (decided 29 October 2026; AGENTS.md).
Secondary-data declaration: the investigators analyzed these files before this plan was written, and the results are published (Swaminathan et al. 2025).

4. Study populations
Candidates. All candidates who consented to the center’s HOPE listing during the study period (23 in the paper). No exclusions are applied.
Offers. All offers from D+ donors to those candidates from March 2018 to April 2022 (122 offers from 85 donors to 12 candidates in the paper). Record-level processing, in order, none of which is an exclusion of a candidate:

The match date is read as a date.
Duplicate offers of the same donor to the same candidate (same candidate ID and donor ID) are reduced to one, keeping the first row.
One accepted offer is recoded as a provisional acceptance, because the recipient became ineligible before transplant. The record and the reason are in the restricted corrections file.

5. Exposure: intervention period
Each offer and each candidate-day is assigned to the pre- or post-intervention period by comparison with day 0, the intervention date, read from the restricted parameters file:

an offer is post-intervention when its match date is after day 0;
a candidate-day is post-intervention when the day starts after day 0.

The paper describes the periods by month (section 2). The code uses the exact intervention date, so its boundary need not fall at the start of a month; where the two differ, the code is followed.

6. Comparator
The pre-intervention period.

7. Outcomes
Offer level.

Offer acceptance: No, Provisional Acceptance, or Yes, as recorded (after the correction in section 4).
Primary refusal reason: the OPTN refusal code recorded for the offer.
Potentially HIV-related decline: among offers with acceptance No, a primary refusal reason in the list below; missing for offers not declined. The list is as in the code, which matches the four codes the paper names, with the first under the name it has in the data (the paper calls it “Donor quality”):

“Donor age or quality”
“Donor medical history, specify”
“Donor social history”
“Positive infectious disease screening test: CMV, HBV, HCV, etc.”

Donor organ transplanted: at least one kidney from the offer’s donor was transplanted, at any center; a missing count is counted as not transplanted.

Candidate level.

Follow-up: each candidate contributes one record per day from the consent date to the end of follow-up (the number of days between them).
Transplant: a transplant is counted on the day whose end equals the transplant date; all other days count 0.
D+/R+ transplant: as for transplant, counting only transplants from D+ donors.
End status: not transplanted; transplanted from a D+ donor; transplanted from a D− donor.

8. Statistical analysis
All analyses use R; the version used for each run is recorded with its outputs.
Offer characteristics (paper Table 2). Counts of distinct candidates and distinct donors with offers. The offer variables of section 7 summarized overall and by period, with tests by period, using gtsummary defaults: n (%) for categorical variables and range for the match date; Wilcoxon rank-sum for the date, and Pearson’s chi-squared or Fisher’s exact test for categorical variables, as gtsummary chooses.
Declined offers. The same summary restricted to offers with acceptance No. Among declined offers, the share whose donor organ was transplanted, by period and by whether the decline was potentially HIV-related.
Transplant rates. Poisson regression of the daily transplant indicator on period, one record per candidate-day, so that the rate is per candidate-day; the incidence rate ratio (post vs pre) with its 95% confidence interval and P value, as reported by gtsummary::tbl_regression(exponentiate = TRUE). Two models: all transplants, and D+/R+ transplants.
Open: standard errors that account for repeated days within a candidate (the original Stata code clustered by candidate; the published R models did not), as an addition to the published models (#3).
Candidate characteristics (paper Supplemental Table 1). Recipient age, sex, race, ethnicity, hepatitis C serology, time on dialysis (years plus months divided by 12), panel reactive antibody class I, and class II as zero or greater than zero, by end status, with an overall column: median (IQR) and n (%), with gtsummary default tests.
Donor and transplant characteristics (paper Supplemental Table 2). Among transplanted candidates, by donor HIV status: warm ischemia time (minutes), cold ischemia time (hours plus minutes divided by 60), donor sex, race, ethnicity, hepatitis C serology and age, donation after brain or cardiac death, and terminal creatinine; median (IQR) and n (%), with gtsummary default tests.
Open: whether the original code’s alternative tables with means (SD), one-way ANOVA and t-tests, which were not published, are kept as unpublished extras or dropped (#4).
Patient timeline (paper Supplemental Figure 1). For each candidate, follow-up before and after day 0 as line segments, with offers (declined; accepted but not transplanted; accepted and transplanted) and end events (transplant from a D− donor, death, permanent delisting, end of study period) as points, on a time axis of days from day 0. Published only as set out in section 10.
Missing data. Analyses use the records as they are; no imputation. Each table reports missing values as gtsummary does by default.

9. Sensitivity analyses
None were published. Any addition (for example #3) is decided in its issue and labelled as not in the paper.

10. Disclosure control
The data are covered by the IRB-approved study protocol. In addition, for patient privacy (decided 29 October 2026):

Restricted values. The intervention date, any person-level date, record identifiers, and the timeline’s random seed are never in the repository. With exact day offsets, the intervention date would give each candidate’s event dates. The code reads them from the restricted folder, and this plan and the website describe each in words.
Patient timeline. The published Supplemental Figure 1 is a static image, from which event times can be read to within about two days. Nothing published here is more precise than what is already public: the timeline may be shown interactively only with each event moved by its own random shift of up to ±2 days, from a seed kept with the restricted values, since a public seed would let the shifts be regenerated and removed.
Small cells. Until the decider sets a small-cell rule, nothing derived from the data is published except numbers that appear in the paper.

Open: a small-cell rule for any output not in the paper (#5).

11. Limitations to address in reporting

A before-and-after design at one center cannot separate the intervention from secular trends, including national growth in D+ organ use (Werbel et al. 2022; Liang et al. 2024) and changes in OPTN allocation during the study period.
Potentially HIV-related declines are inferred from OPTN refusal codes that were not designed to record HIV status; in particular the donor quality code is broad.
Small numbers: 23 candidates, 122 offers and 7 D+/R+ transplants, giving wide confidence intervals.
The Poisson models treat each candidate-day as independent (#3).
The post-intervention period overlaps the COVID-19 pandemic, which affected refusal reasons and candidate availability.

The project
This repository releases the analysis code of a published single-center study of a multispecialty educational intervention, delivered in December 2020, to increase acceptance of organs from donors with HIV for recipients with HIV under the HOPE Act (Swaminathan et al., Transpl Infect Dis 2025;e70039, doi:10.1111/tid.70039). The study compares the periods before and after the intervention: organ offers and the reasons they were declined, the rate of transplants per patient-year on the waiting list, and the characteristics of candidates and transplants. The original analysis was one R Markdown file, kept in original/ with its restricted values removed. This repository rebuilds it as scripts and publishes the code and methods as a Quarto website. No patient-level data, and no results beyond those in the published paper, are in the repository.

analysis-plan.md is the source of truth for design. Code implements the plan; it does not redefine it. If code needs to depart from the plan, open a decision issue, or comment on the existing one, for the decider. Once the decider has settled it (in the issue, or relayed there in his exact words), the plan change and the code can go in the same pull request, which closes the issue.
Decider. Scientific decisions are made by Vagish Hemmige, in every area. Anyone may open or contribute to a decision issue; only the decider settles it (see “Working with agents”).
Replication rule. The original code is evidence of what was done, not the specification. By default the rebuilt code reproduces the published numbers. When the original code disagrees with the paper or contains an error, do not silently copy it or silently fix it: the site’s “Differences from the original code” page records every difference, and any change from what was published goes to a decision issue.
This is an analysis project, not an R package. Do not add DESCRIPTION, NAMESPACE, roxygen, or pkgdown infrastructure, or apply CRAN conventions.
Default branch: master, protected. Changes reach it only through pull requests.

To allow more for a source, a person changes its row through a pull request, naming the agreement and section that permit it, the approved AI service, and exactly what agents may do. Agents never propose or make this change themselves, and nothing in personal instructions can grant it.
For every package used: read its documentation before relying on behavior that sets a denominator, a period, an outcome, or a test, rather than assuming it from a function’s name. Work around a package’s problems in R/functions.R, with a comment explaining the problem and linking any upstream issue. Reporting a bug upstream is an external communication; the person directing the work decides whether to file it.
For these sources (no package): one loading script reads each file, records its name and the date in its name, and does any processing in labelled steps. A replacement file gets a new dated name, and the loading script and the plan change in the same pull request. Column names and types are checked when read, so a changed file stops the run instead of being silently misread.

The offers’ refusal reasons are OPTN refusal codes, matched as text. The list of codes counted as potentially HIV-related is a named constant in R/setup.R, with each code exactly as it appears in the data.

Exploration and definitive analysis
Exploration is welcome on branches or forks. Experimental scripts need not be sourced from R/main.R or have Quarto pages, and their findings are labelled preliminary. A script becomes part of the definitive analysis when it is sourced from R/main.R; from then on every rule below applies to it.

R scripts

Running the analysis. Run R/main.R from the project root. It sources the other scripts in dependency order; ARCHITECTURE.md describes what each does.
One job per script. When you add a definitive script, source it from main.R at the right point and update ARCHITECTURE.md in the same pull request.
Header comment. Each script begins with what it does, which objects it needs from earlier scripts, and what it produces.
Constants, libraries, and code lists live in R/setup.R. Other scripts do not call library(), re-source setup.R, or hard-code values. Any number a reader might want to change (a threshold, a period boundary, a list of codes) is a named constant there.
Helper functions go in R/functions.R. A function takes its inputs as arguments and does not read global objects.
No side effects outside the project. No setwd(), absolute paths, or writes outside the project. Restricted files are located only through the data-raw/ paths defined in R/setup.R.
No restricted values in tracked files. The intervention date, the timeline’s jitter seed, any person-level date, and any record identifier (match ID, PX_ID, donor ID, Study_ID values) never appear in code, comments, the site, commit messages, issues or pull-request text. Code reads the date from data-raw/restricted-parameters.yml and applies corrections listed in data-raw/record-corrections.csv; the plan and the site describe each one in words and say it was removed for patient privacy. The study period may be described as in the paper (March 2018 to November 2020, December 2020 to April 2022).
No results in the repository. No script (exploratory or definitive) or comment, commit message, issue, pull-request text or review report contains results, counts or data values from the restricted data unless they are cleared for release. Check before every commit and post, since a public repository publishes everything pushed to it, on any branch. Numbers quoted from the published paper are public and may be cited.

Chunk labels
Scripts are divided into labelled sections so Quarto pages can show the code without copying it:
## ---- <step-name>

Every logical step has a label. A label covers the code from its line to the next label.
Labels are kebab-case, describe the step, and are unique across all scripts; a duplicate silently picks up the wrong code.
Search the .qmd files before renaming or deleting a label.
Labels are comments and never change what the code does.

Variable labels
Label analysis variables with human-readable descriptions using labelled::set_variable_labels(). Label each derived variable where it is created, with units (days, years, hours) and the period it refers to.

Quarto website
The site documents the code. It does not run the analysis.

_quarto.yml and index.qmd sit at the root; quarto/ has one page per definitive script, named after it. The custom-callout extension in _extensions/ provides the Rcode callout.
Each page loads its script with knitr::read_chunk("../R/<script>.R") in a hidden chunk and shows each labelled section with #| eval: false, with prose explaining what the section does and why. Pages link to the script on GitHub and to the scripts it depends on.
Never evaluate analysis code in the site. Pages render without restricted data.
The original R Markdown file is shown on its own page as code only. The page says which lines and header fields were edited for publication and why.
The site renders to docs/ and is served by GitHub Pages. When you add a script, add its page and sidebar entry in the same pull request, and re-render.
Prose must match the code. If a change alters what a section does, update its explanation in the same pull request.

Outputs

Tables and figures are exported by R/tables.R and R/figures.R to tables/ and figures/. They are gitignored until the decider has checked them against the published paper and cleared them for release under the disclosure rules below.
No figure is more precise than the published one. Interactive figures (for example plotly or other htmlwidgets) embed every data point, so the patient timeline is published only with each event moved by its own random shift of up to ±2 days, the precision of the published static figure (decided 29 October 2026; see the plan). The seed for those shifts is a restricted value, kept in data-raw/restricted-parameters.yml: with the seed, the shifts could be regenerated and subtracted.
Published figures need alt text.
README.Rmd is the source of README.md; edit the .Rmd and re-knit.

Restricted data (applies to everyone)
The Access column of “Data sources” says which sources are restricted. For each restricted source:

Never commit data, extracts, or saved objects or outputs derived from patient-level records. data-raw/ sits inside the project folder but is ignored by Git; check .gitignore before adding a new output type. Ignoring a folder does not stop anyone, or any tool connected to the folder, from reading it.
AI agents never read restricted data. Anything an agent opens, prints, or summarizes is sent to the model provider. Agents do not open data files or patient-level objects, print rows, or display identifiers or person-level dates. Agents also do not open outputs from restricted data that are not yet cleared for release (tables/ and figures/ while they are ignored). Because data-raw/ is inside the project folder, the project folder is never connected to an AI tool. Agents write code, review it, and run it on synthetic data; results on real data are produced by an authorized person.
Synthetic data are built in code, labelled as synthetic, and never derived from real records.
Person-level dates. Dates of consent, offers, transplant, death and delisting are identifiers. No published output lets them be recovered more precisely than the published paper already allows; for the patient timeline, that is ±2 days (see Outputs).
Disclosure. Until the decider sets a small-cell rule for this project, nothing derived from the restricted data is published except numbers that appear in the published paper (decided 29 October 2026). Check every output before it leaves the approved environment, including scripts, comments, commit messages, issues, pull-request text and review reports (see R scripts).
Credentials. Never commit keys, tokens, or .Renviron.

Coding conventions

Cohort flow. Any exclusion of candidates or offers goes through the flowchart package (fc_filter()), in the plan’s order, so counts and data come from the same code. Record-level processing (removing duplicate offers of one donor to one candidate, applying a listed correction, expanding follow-up into person-days) is not an exclusion, and is done in labelled steps with a check of the rows before and after. An analysis that uses fewer people or offers than its cohort reports its own number with that analysis.
Code lists (refusal codes) carry each code exactly as it appears in the data and the reason it is included. Never invent codes, variables, files, or definitions.
Joins use join_by() with an explicit relationship where possible. After every join of records to people, assert that rows did not multiply, and decide deliberately what happens to unmatched rows. Offers are linked to candidates by last name, as in the original code (decided 29 October 2026). Linking by an identifier would be better practice, and the differences page says so; names stay inside the join, are dropped straight after it, and are never printed, labelled, or written to an output.
Dates and periods are compared with the intervention date read from the restricted file, with the boundary rule (strictly after, or on and after) written as in the plan, and the edges are tested on synthetic data.
Code that turns model output into reported numbers lives in named functions in R/functions.R, tested on synthetic data with a known answer.
Style: readable tidyverse code, following the tidyverse style guide: dplyr pipelines (|>), one step per line; case_when(.default = ) rather than nested ifelse(); select by name, never by position; checks are a filter() of the problem rows followed by stop() with a message that says what failed. Style changes go in their own commits.

Checks for any change
Check the items that apply before opening a pull request.

Plan: does the change implement the plan as written, and does it leave every open decision open?
Cohort: do the flowchart steps’ order, denominators, and labels match their conditions, and can each count be reproduced from code?
Joins and denominators: no unintended row multiplication; missing and zero kept distinct.
Reported numbers: does each estimate match the plan’s estimand, and do tables, figures, and site prose say what the code actually computes?
Structure: is ARCHITECTURE.md current; are chunk labels unique and found by their pages; does every definitive script have a page and sidebar entry; does any site chunk run analysis code? Only the hidden read_chunk() import, and results pages reading outputs cleared for release, run.
Execution: does main.R run in a fresh session with relative paths; are any saved intermediates or caches stale?

Project-specific checks:

Privacy sweep: search every changed tracked file for dates, record identifiers, names and absolute paths. Only the paper’s study-period months may appear, and made-up values in synthetic test data, in files labelled as synthetic (decided 29 October 2026).
Replication: does every difference from the original code appear on the differences page, and is each one either reproducing the published code or linked to a decision issue?
Periods: is each offer and each person-day assigned to the pre- or post-intervention period by the plan’s boundary rule, tested at the boundary?
Person-time: does the expansion into person-days give each candidate exactly the days from consent to end of follow-up, with each transplant counted once, on the right day?
Offers: are duplicate offers of one donor to one candidate removed as the plan says, and are corrections applied only from the restricted list?

Working with agents

Autonomy. The person directing an agent decides how much it may do, and may give it stricter rules of their own; those take precedence. By default an agent may edit code and documentation, add scripts and tests, run code and render the site on synthetic data, and commit to a branch and open a pull request.
Decisions. Anyone, including an agent, may add options and evidence to a decision issue. The decider states the choice in the issue. Agents implement decisions; they never choose among options on their own, in the issue, the plan, or the code.
Every agent, under any autonomy: never merges a pull request; follows the restricted-data rules; asks before running the full pipeline or making expensive calls; and shows a person the exact text before posting or sending anything as them, unless that person’s own instructions waive this.
Pull requests opened by an agent are focused. Each says which plan section or issue it addresses, what was checked, and whether by running code on synthetic data or by reading only. Synthetic results are never described as results.
References: cite the source documentation and literature used, in references.bib.

title: 5. Models
text: Fits the Poisson models of transplant rate after versus before the intervention, as published (analysis plan, section 8).

title: 5. Models
text:
Poisson models
One row per candidate-day, so the rate is per candidate-day and the exponentiated coefficient is the incidence rate ratio, post- versus pre-intervention. One model counts all transplants and the other only transplants from donors with HIV. As published, the models do not account for repeated days within a candidate; standard errors that do are an open decision (#3).


Click to show/hide R Code
# Poisson GLM, all transplants as outcome
m1 <- glm(Transplant_Outcome ~ Post_Intervention, family = "poisson",
          data = transplant_data_processed)

# Poisson GLM, HIV D+ transplants as outcome
m2 <- glm(HIV_Transplant_Outcome ~ Post_Intervention, family = "poisson",
          data = transplant_data_processed)

title: About
text:
This repository
This repository releases the code behind the published analysis, rebuilt from a single R Markdown file into scripts run in order by R/main.R. The study data are identifiable and covered by the IRB-approved study protocol; they are not in the repository, and the code reads them from a restricted folder on the computer of an authorized analyst. The values that could identify patients were removed from the code and are kept with the data.
Contributions follow the rules in AGENTS.md; open decisions and known issues are tracked in Issues.

title: About
text:
How this website was created
The site is built with Quarto from the analysis scripts themselves. Each page imports the labelled sections of its script from R/ and shows them with an explanation; the site never runs the analysis, so it is built without the restricted study data.
The repository was set up, and is maintained, with the R Analysis Workflow plugin for AI coding assistants (Claude and ChatGPT), written by Vagish Hemmige. The plugin provides the repository layout, the conventions for the analysis plan and AGENTS.md, and the format of these pages. AI assistants (Claude) drafted code, documentation and suggestions under the rules in AGENTS.md: code, documentation and synthetic data; the study data stayed on the maintainer’s computer, and only published or summary outputs were shared with them for checking. Every scientific decision was made by the decider and recorded in a GitHub issue or in the analysis plan.
Four documents describe the project. In short: the plan is the scientific intent, the architecture is the workflow as implemented, and AGENTS.md holds the rules for working together.

Analysis plan: what the analysis is meant to do, and why. The question, the populations, the measures, the statistical methods, and the choices that need the investigators’ judgment, with each open choice linked to its decision issue. Code implements it and does not redefine it.
Architecture: how the code does it. The scripts, the order they run in, what each needs and produces, and how data flow between them.
AGENTS.md: how people and AI assistants work on the project. Rules for restricted data and patient privacy, coding, testing, proposing changes and getting a person’s approval.
Repository blueprint: the intended layout, which the architecture document then describes as built.

title: Setup
text:
Restricted values
The intervention date and the timeline’s random seed are read from data-raw/restricted-parameters.yml, and the record corrections from data-raw/record-corrections.csv. They are kept out of the code for patient privacy: with the exact intervention date, the day offsets in the analysis would give each patient’s event dates, and with the seed, the timeline’s shifts could be regenerated and removed. The step checks that each file has what the analysis needs and never prints the values.


Click to show/hide R Code

# restricted folder, not in the code: with exact day offsets, the intervention
# date would give each candidate's event dates, and a public seed would let the
# timeline's shifts be regenerated and removed. Their values are never printed.
check_files_exist(c(restricted_parameters_file, record_corrections_file))

restricted_parameters <- read_yaml(restricted_parameters_file)
check_names_present(
  names(restricted_parameters),
  c("intervention_date", "timeline_jitter_seed"),
  restricted_parameters_file
)
InterventionDate <- ymd(restricted_parameters$intervention_date, quiet = TRUE)
if (is.na(InterventionDate)) {
  stop("intervention_date in ", restricted_parameters_file,
       " is not a date written as YYYY-MM-DD.", call. = FALSE)
}
timeline_jitter_seed <- as.integer(restricted_parameters$timeline_jitter_seed)
if (is.na(timeline_jitter_seed)) {
  stop("timeline_jitter_seed in ", restricted_parameters_file,
       " is not a whole number.", call. = FALSE)
}
rm(restricted_parameters)

# Record-level corrections: one row per corrected value, with the reason.
record_corrections <- read_csv(
  record_corrections_file,
  col_types = cols(.default = col_character())
)
check_names_present(
  names(record_corrections),
  c("source", "record_id", "field", "corrected_value", "reason"),
  record_corrections_file
)

title: Clinical background
text: People with HIV are more likely than others to develop kidney failure (Abraham et al. 2015), and once on dialysis they are less likely to receive a kidney transplant (Locke et al. 2017; Blumberg and Rogers 2019). South African surgeons showed that kidneys from deceased donors with HIV could be transplanted into recipients with HIV with good results (Muller et al. 2015). In the United States, the HIV Organ Policy Equity (HOPE) Act of 2013 made this legal, under research protocols (Doby et al. 2018). The multicenter HOPE in Action studies that followed found outcomes after kidney transplantation from donors with HIV similar to those from donors without HIV (Durand et al. 2021, 2024). After liver transplantation, a smaller pilot study found similar graft survival, rejection and HIV breakthrough, but lower one-year patient survival and more opportunistic infections and cancers with donors with HIV (Durand et al. 2022). Candidates with HIV who were willing to accept these kidneys also waited less time for a transplant (Motter et al. 2024).

title: Clinical background
section: Why organs from donors with HIV went unused
text:
Why organs from donors with HIV went unused
Use of organs from donors with HIV has been lower than expected, nationally (Boyarsky et al. 2011; Liang et al. 2024) and, before the intervention, at this center (Swaminathan et al. 2025). The center has large HIV and kidney transplant programs, and its candidates with HIV received offers from donors with HIV, but it performed only one transplant from a donor with HIV between March 2018 and November 2020, and many of the organs it declined were transplanted at other centers. Reviewing how offers had been discussed, and asking the transplant teams, identified concerns such as the risks of HIV in the donor, unfamiliarity with the outcome data, and lack of support for difficult decisions out of hours.

title: Clinical background
text:
The intervention
In December 2020 the center introduced a multispecialty educational intervention (Swaminathan et al. 2025): teaching sessions on outcomes of transplantation from donors with HIV for infectious diseases and transplant staff and leadership; enrolling all transplant infectious diseases physicians in the offer notifications; talks by colleagues from experienced centers; and monthly multidisciplinary meetings reviewing every offer from a donor with HIV in a standard format.

title: Clinical background
text:
What the analysis measures
The analysis compares the periods before and after the intervention. For offers, it measures how often offers were accepted, the refusal codes recorded for declined offers, and whether a declined organ was transplanted elsewhere. Because refusal codes do not record HIV status, four codes are counted as a potentially HIV-related decline. For candidates, it measures the rate of transplants per time on the waiting list, all transplants and transplants from donors with HIV. The analysis plan defines each measure.

title: A multispecialty educational intervention to improve acceptance of organs from donors with HIV: the analysis code
text:
What this site does
The original analysis was a single R Markdown file (shown here). This repository rebuilds it as scripts that R/main.R runs in order, and this site explains each script step by step. The rebuilt code is written to reproduce the published numbers; every place where it differs from the original code, or where the paper differs from the code, is listed on the differences page.






NotePatient privacy



The code is published without the values that could identify patients. The intervention date (day 0 for both study periods), one record-level correction and the random seed used by the patient timeline are kept with the restricted study data, not in the code. With the exact intervention date, the day offsets in the analysis would give each patient’s event dates. The correction recodes one accepted offer as a provisional acceptance, because the recipient became ineligible before transplant. The patient timeline moves each event by up to two days, so it is no more precise than the published figure.

title: A multispecialty educational intervention to improve acceptance of organs from donors with HIV: the analysis code
text:
Methods
The authoritative specification is the analysis plan. In brief: a single-center before-and-after comparison. Offers from donors with HIV to the center’s candidates are compared by period, including declines for refusal codes considered potentially HIV-related. Transplant rates are compared with Poisson regression on one record per candidate per day of follow-up. Candidate, donor and transplant characteristics are compared by whether and how candidates were transplanted.

title: 2. Person-days
text:
One row per day
Each candidate contributes one row per day from consent to the end of follow-up; day k starts k − 1 days after consent and ends k days after. Follow-up must be measured in days: R chooses the units of a difference between date-times from the smallest one in the column, so a candidate with less than a day of follow-up would make every candidate expand into seconds. The step stops in that case.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Each candidate contributes one row per day from consent to the end of
# follow-up. Day k starts k - 1 days after consent and ends k days after.
# The original code's duration is End_Date - Date_of_consent, whose units R
# chooses from the smallest difference in the column: days when every
# candidate has at least a day of follow-up, but seconds if any candidate has
# none, which would expand every candidate into seconds. Stop rather than
# reproduce that; the published analysis must have had days.
follow_up_length <- transplant_data_unprocessed$End_Date - transplant_data_unprocessed$Date_of_consent
if (units(follow_up_length) != "days") {
  stop("Follow-up lengths are in ", units(follow_up_length),
       ", not days, because a candidate has less than a day of follow-up. ",
       "The original code would expand follow-up incorrectly.", call. = FALSE)
}
rm(follow_up_length)

  mutate(duration = as.numeric(End_Date - Date_of_consent)) %>%
  uncount(duration) %>%
  group_by(Study_ID) %>%
  mutate(start_date = days(row_number()) + Date_of_consent - days(1),
         stop_date = days(row_number()) + Date_of_consent)

text:
Day jitter
Moves each day offset by its own random whole number of days, from minus to plus the given maximum. A shift that would carry an event across day 0 is applied in the opposite direction instead, so every event stays in its own period, matching how periods are assigned (after day 0 is post-intervention). The seed is set only inside the function, so the shifts are the same on every run and nothing else in the session is affected.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Shift each day offset from day 0 by its own random whole number of days, from
# -max_days to max_days, all equally likely. A shift never moves a value to
# the other side of day 0 (decided 29 October 2026): values at or before day 0
# stay at or before it, and values after it stay after it, matching how the
# periods are assigned (post-intervention means after day 0). A shift that
# would cross is applied in the opposite direction instead. Missing values
# stay missing. The seed is set only inside this function, so the shifts are
# the same on every run and nothing else in the session is affected.
jitter_days <- function(x, max_days, seed) {
  shifts <- withr::with_seed(
    seed,
    sample(seq(-max_days, max_days), length(x), replace = TRUE)
  )
  shifted <- x + shifts
  crossed <- !is.na(x) & ((x <= 0) != (shifted <= 0))
  shifted[crossed] <- x[crossed] - shifts[crossed]
  shifted
}

# Turn a column into a factor whose levels keep the order they would have by
# default (sorted), with some levels shown under new names. `labels` is a
# named vector: names are the values as they appear in the data, values the
# names to show. Values not in the data are ignored. Used only for display.
relabel_levels <- function(x, labels = character()) {
  values <- sort(unique(x))
  shown <- as.character(values)
  matched <- shown %in% names(labels)
  shown[matched] <- labels[shown[matched]]
  factor(x, levels = values, labels = shown)
}

Link to study IDs
Offers are linked to candidates’ study IDs by last name, as in the original code. An identifier would be better practice; the name is used only inside this step and dropped straight after. The original join used every column the two tables share, which is only the last name when the offers have no study ID column, so the step checks that, and stops if the join would duplicate offers.

# code (decided 29 October 2026; an identifier would be better practice).
# The original join used every column the two tables share; that is only the

title: Figures
text:
Follow-up
Days from day 0 to each candidate’s consent and end of follow-up. Each is moved by its own random shift of up to two days, never across day 0, so the figure is no more precise than the published static one; the interactive page embeds every plotted value, which is why the shift comes before plotting. The end of follow-up is one event, so its shifted day is used for both the end of the line and the end marker.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Days from day 0 to each candidate's consent and end of follow-up, each
# shifted at random. The end of follow-up is one event: its shifted day is used
# both for the end of the candidate's line and for its end-of-follow-up point.
timeline_follow_up <- transplant_data_unprocessed %>%
  transmute(
    Study_ID,
    consent_day = as.numeric(as.Date(Date_of_consent) - as.Date(InterventionDate)),
    end_day = as.numeric(as.Date(End_Date) - as.Date(InterventionDate))
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    consent_day = jitter_days(consent_day, timeline_jitter_days, timeline_jitter_seed),
    end_day = jitter_days(end_day, timeline_jitter_days, timeline_jitter_seed + 1L)
  )

title: Figures
text:
Events
Offers, as declined, accepted but not transplanted, or accepted and transplanted, each at its own shifted day; and how follow-up ended for candidates not transplanted from a donor with HIV.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Offers, as declined, accepted but not transplanted, or accepted and
# transplanted, each at its own shifted day.
graphic_data_points_1 <- organ_offers_processed %>%
  mutate(Event = case_when(
    Offer_Acceptance == "No" ~ "HIV offer declined",
    Offer_Acceptance == "Provisional Acceptance" ~ "HIV offer accepted, but not transplanted",
    Offer_Acceptance == "Yes" ~ "HIV offer accepted and transplanted")) %>%
  mutate(endpoint = as.numeric(as.Date(Match_Date) - as.Date(InterventionDate))) %>%
  mutate(endpoint = jitter_days(endpoint, timeline_jitter_days, timeline_jitter_seed + 2L)) %>%
  select(Study_ID, endpoint, Event)

# How follow-up ended, for candidates not transplanted from a donor with HIV,
# at the shifted end of follow-up.
graphic_data_points_2 <- transplant_data_unprocessed %>%
  filter(HIV_transplanted == 0) %>%
  mutate(Event = case_when(
    Transplanted == 1 & HIV_transplanted == 0 ~ "Non-HIV offer accepted and transplanted",
    str_detect(Listing_Status, "Deceased") ~ "Death",
    str_detect(Listing_Status, "Withdrawn") ~ "Permanently delisted",
    TRUE ~ "End of study period")) %>%
  select(Study_ID, Event) %>%
  left_join(select(timeline_follow_up, Study_ID, endpoint = end_day),
            by = "Study_ID", relationship = "one-to-one")

graphic_data_points <- bind_rows(graphic_data_points_1, graphic_data_points_2) %>%
  mutate(Study_ID = as.factor(Study_ID))

rm(graphic_data_points_1, graphic_data_points_2)

title: Figures
text:
Lines
Each candidate’s follow-up as up to two segments split at day 0: red before the intervention and blue after, as in the original code.


Click to show/hide R Code
# Each candidate's follow-up as up to two segments, split at day 0: before the
# intervention (red) and after it (blue). The split logic is the original code's.
graphic_data_lines <- timeline_follow_up %>%
  rename(endpoint_left = consent_day, endpoint_right = end_day) %>%
  mutate(endpoint1_left = case_when(
    endpoint_left < 0 ~ endpoint_left,
    endpoint_left >= 0 ~ NA_real_)) %>%
  mutate(endpoint1_right = case_when(
    endpoint_left < 0 & endpoint_right > 0 ~ 0,
    endpoint_left < 0 & endpoint_right < 0 ~ endpoint_right,
    endpoint_left >= 0 ~ NA_real_)) %>%
  mutate(endpoint2_left = case_when(
    endpoint_left < 0 & endpoint_right > 0 ~ 0,
    endpoint_left > 0 & endpoint_right > 0 ~ endpoint_left,
    endpoint_right <= 0 ~ NA_real_)) %>%
  mutate(endpoint2_right = case_when(
    endpoint_right > 0 ~ endpoint_right,
    endpoint_right <= 0 ~ NA_real_)) %>%
  select(Study_ID, endpoint1_left, endpoint1_right, endpoint2_left, endpoint2_right) %>%
  mutate(Study_ID = as.factor(Study_ID))

Analytical scripts

R/main.R sources the definitive scripts in dependency order.
Workflow: functions and setup → loading → processing (offers, person-days, demographics) → models → tables and figures.
R/tables.R and R/figures.R generate the outputs directly.

Documentation

Document definitive analytical scripts with explanatory Quarto pages; exploratory scripts need not have pages.
Use Dialysis-facility-density-USRDS as the example for a site that documents a published analysis, and Cryptococcus-cost-analysis for Quarto supporting files, chunk imports, callouts and formatting; neither for scientific methods.

Outputs and version control

Outputs from the restricted data stay local and out of Git until the decider has checked them against the paper and cleared them for release (AGENTS.md).
.gitignore: excludes data-raw/, Archive/, any copy of the original code that still holds the restricted values, data formats, Stata logs, Word, PDF and HTML files outside docs/, figures/, tables/, credentials and caches. Ignoring a folder does not stop anyone, or any connected tool, from reading it.
